Variance functions for heteroscedastic residuals

Source: R/varFunc.R
varFunc.Rd

Variance functions for the variance argument of gcTMB, with the arguments and the parameterisation of varIdent, varPower, varConstPower, varExp and varComb of the package nlme (whose objects gcTMB also accepts), and the polynomial varPoly, for the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families. The residual variance of an observation is sigma^2 g^2, with the residual standard deviation sigma of the model and the function g:

  • varIdent(form=~ 1 | s): g = delta_s, a ratio for each stratum s of the grouping variables, with delta = 1 for the reference stratum, so that each stratum has its own variance, e.g. a variance for each treatment (~ 1 | Treatment) or for each time point (~ 1 | Time); a numeric grouping variable is treated as a factor;

  • varPower(form=~ v): g = |v|^delta, variance sigma^2 |v|^(2 delta);

  • varConstPower(form=~ v): g = c + |v|^delta, c > 0, variance sigma^2 (c + |v|^delta)^2;

  • varExp(form=~ v): g = exp(t v), variance sigma^2 exp(2 t v);

  • varPoly(form=~ v, degree=k): g = 1 + d_1 (v - m) + d_2 (v - m)^2 + ... + d_k (v - m)^k, so that the standard deviation sigma g is a polynomial in v, e.g. one that is largest in the middle of the range of v (d_1 > 0, d_2 < 0, with its maximum at v = m - d_1/(2 d_2) for degree 2). The polynomial is centred at the mean m of v in the data (the mean response for fitted(.), m = 0 for rate(.)), shown by print, so that sigma is the standard deviation at v = m, and the standard deviation at v = 0 can take any value; an uncentred polynomial, with sigma the standard deviation at v = 0, could not describe a standard deviation that would be 0 or below at v = 0 but is positive on the data, e.g. a straight line in the time from the first day. A polynomial can be 0 or negative, where the standard deviation is not defined: the likelihood is zero (the log-likelihood minus infinity) if the polynomial is 0 or below at any observation, so that the optimiser stays where it is positive on the data. It starts from d = 0, a constant standard deviation. Outside the data, e.g. in predict and simulate at new times, the polynomial can still be 0 or below, which gives an error. A degree above 2 is rarely needed and tends to overfit;

  • varComb(...): the product of the multipliers g of two or more of the above, e.g. varComb(varIdent(form=~ 1 | Treatment), varPower()) for a power of the fitted curve with a different factor for each treatment, or varComb(varPower(), varExp()), g = |v|^delta exp(t v), which with delta > 0 and t < 0 is largest at v = -delta/t, in the middle of growth. The variances are multiplied, not added: the standard deviations are sigma g_A g_B.

The covariate v of varPower and varConstPower is a numeric variable of the data, e.g. ~ Time, fitted(.) (the default), the fitted curve f(t) of each observation (with its random effects), or rate(.), the growth rate f'(t) of the fitted curve at the time of the observation, its slope, which is largest at the inflection point. rate(.) is a gcTMB addition, not available in nlme; it is computed by a central difference. With a grouping factor, form=~ v | g, each level of g has its own power (and constant).

Usage

varIdent(value = numeric(0), form = ~1, fixed = NULL)

varPower(value = numeric(0), form = ~fitted(.), fixed = NULL)

varConstPower(
  const = numeric(0),
  power = numeric(0),
  form = ~fitted(.),
  fixed = NULL
)

varExp(value = numeric(0), form = ~fitted(.), fixed = NULL)

varPoly(value = numeric(0), degree = 2, form = ~fitted(.), fixed = NULL)

varComb(...)

Arguments

value

Numeric. Starting values (or with fixed, see there): for varIdent the ratios of the standard deviations of the strata to the reference stratum, named by stratum (1 by default); for varPower the power and for varExp the exponent t (0 by default), named by level with a grouping factor; for varPoly the coefficients d_1, ..., d_k (0 by default), one for each power of v, or named poly1, ..., polyk (poly1:<level> for a single level of a grouping factor)

form

One-sided formula: ~ 1 | s for varIdent, with s one or more grouping variables (~ 1 | A * B); ~ v or ~ v | g for varPower, varConstPower, varExp and varPoly, with v a numeric variable, fitted(.) or rate(.)

fixed

Values that are fixed and not estimated: for varIdent ratios named by stratum, for varPower the power and for varExp the exponent (named by level with a grouping factor), for varConstPower a list with const and/or power, e.g. fixed=list(power=1), for varPoly coefficients named as in value, e.g. fixed=c(poly2=0)

const, power

Numeric. For varConstPower, the starting values of the constant c (0.1 by default, as nlme) and the power delta (0 by default)

degree

Integer. The degree k of the polynomial of varPoly, 2 by default

...

For varComb, two or more variance functions, whose standard deviation multipliers g are multiplied

Value

An object of class c("varIdent", "varFunc"), c("varPower", "varFunc"), c("varConstPower", "varFunc"), c("varExp", "varFunc"), c("varPoly", "varFunc") or c("varComb", "varFunc"), with the structure of the nlme objects (a list of the components for varComb).

Details

The variance of varPower goes to zero where |v| does, e.g. the fitted values of a curve that starts at zero or the growth rate before and after growth, which makes those observations too influential and the fit unstable; varConstPower keeps the variance at least sigma^2 c^2 there. A negative power gives an infinite variance at |v| = 0; with rate(.), this is the case for curves whose growth rate passes through zero within the data, such as the beta curve after its maximum, which the optimiser cannot handle, so rate(.) is meant for curves that keep growing. Unlike nlme, which updates the fitted values between fits of the variance parameters, gcTMB computes them inside the likelihood, so the fit is the joint maximum likelihood estimate. The reference stratum of varIdent is the first level of the grouping variables (sorted numerically for a numeric variable), unless value and fixed name all the others; nlme takes the first in the order of the data.

A variance function and a correlation structure can be combined: the correlation is then that of the standardised residuals e/(sigma g). With varIdent(~ 1 | Time), simulate and prediction intervals need the time points of the fit.

The estimated parameters are in coef(fit) as var_par:<stratum> (the log ratios of varIdent), var_par:power, var_par:const (the log of c), var_par:expon and var_par:poly1, var_par:poly2, ..., with :<level> for a grouping factor, on the unconstrained scale of nlme; varpars gives them on the natural scale. The parameters of the components of varComb are prefixed with A., B., ..., as in nlme.

References

Pinheiro, J.C. and Bates, D.M. (2000). Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS. Springer, New York.

See also

gcTMB, varpars, corStruct

Examples

FabaHeights25$trt <- factor(FabaHeights25$Treatment)
# a residual variance for each treatment
fiti <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, fform=b1 ~ trt, data=FabaHeights25, variance=varIdent(form=~ 1 | trt))
varpars(fiti)
#>       0.1       0.3       0.5       0.6       0.8 
#> 1.0000000 0.9576577 0.6382966 0.2639973 0.3899443 
# residual standard deviation c + f'(t)^delta, largest where the curve grows fastest
fitr <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, variance=varConstPower(form=~ rate(.)))
varpars(fitr)
#>     const     power 
#>  2.834950 -2.224761 
# \donttest{
# a standard deviation that is a quadratic polynomial of the fitted curve
fitp <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, variance=varPoly(degree=2))
varpars(fitp)
#>         poly1         poly2 
#>  8.109823e-03 -7.279771e-05 
# the product of a power and an exponential of the fitted curve
fitc <- gcTMB(Height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25, variance=varComb(varPower(), varExp()))
varpars(fitc)
#>      A.power      B.expon 
#>  0.833573792 -0.004632256 
# }
